# How to use this text {.unnumbered}

This is a study text for **SQE1 FLK1**, written against the SRA's Assessment Specification
as it stands from 1 September 2026.

## What this text is for

SQE1 is not an essay exam. It is 360 single-best-answer multiple choice questions across two
papers, at roughly 1.7 minutes each, and it tests whether you can *apply* a rule to a client's
facts rather than whether you can recite it. This text is written to that end. Every chapter
states the rule, explains why it exists, works an example where the rule is mechanical, and then
names the discrimination the examiner is most likely to build a question around.

Three conventions run throughout.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
The wrong answer that looks right. These mark the places where a plausible-sounding option is
offered and most candidates take it.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Verify before relying on this"}
A point that turns on law which has moved recently, or which the author is not fully confident of.
Check it against a current primary source before you commit it to memory.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example"}
A rule applied to facts, step by step, where the mechanics matter more than the statement.
:::

## The examinable law cut-off {#sec-cutoff}

This matters more than it first appears. The SRA fixes an **examinable law cut-off date** for each
sitting: for the July 2026 sitting it was 13 March 2026. Law that comes into force *after* your
sitting's cut-off is **not examinable**, however prominent it is.

The practical consequence is counter-intuitive. Learning the newest reform can lose you marks.
Leasehold, renting and corporate transparency law are all mid-reform, commencing in stages, and it
is entirely possible to learn a rule that is correct in practice and wrong for your paper. Where
this text discusses a reform in progress it says so explicitly and states the pre-reform position
as the examinable one.

::: {.callout-caution title="Confirm your own cut-off"}
Check the cut-off date for your sitting on the SQE website before revising anything time-sensitive.
The date for July 2027 had not been published when this text was written.
:::

## Ethics is not a separate subject

Professional conduct is not examined on its own in SQE1. It is embedded in scenarios across both
papers, which means an otherwise straightforward company law question can turn on the SRA
Principles or the Code of Conduct. This text raises conduct where it arises rather than
quarantining it in a chapter, because that is how it will reach you in the exam.

Where the Principles conflict, those which safeguard the wider public interest — the rule of law
and the proper administration of justice — take precedence over an individual client's interests.
That ordering decides a surprising number of questions.

## Sources

The syllabus structure and assessment objectives are taken from the SRA's SQE1 Assessment
Specification. Statute references are to the legislation as amended. Case citations are given in
full on first use in each chapter.
